paper_a.title: High-dimensional analysis of double descent for linear regression with random projections

paper_b.title: Double Descent Demystified: Identifying, Interpreting & Ablating the Sources of a Deep Learning Puzzle

metadata.description: Both papers analyze the double-descent phenomenon in linear regression. Paper A (Bach) develops a rigorous high-dimensional asymptotic theory via Stieltjes transforms, self-consistent equations, and random matrix tools (Hanson-Wright, Marchenko-Pastur), characterising bias and variance with effective degrees of freedom df_1, df_2 and a self-induced regularizer kappa(lambda). Paper B (Schaeffer et al.) gives a tutorial-style finite-sample SVD decomposition that attributes the test-error spike to the simultaneous extremes of three factors (small sigma_r, residual projection u_r.E, test projection x_test.v_r), validated by ablation experiments. They tackle the same phenomenon from substantially different machinery (asymptotic RMT vs. finite-sample SVD geometry) and so the relationship is best described as competing/complementary frameworks rather than alternative proofs of the same theorem. Despite the hint AP, the JSON evidence shows distinct objects of study and distinct theorems, which fits CF more cleanly.

matches.explanation: Both papers set up the same linear regression problem on i.i.d. covariates with a linear predictor. Paper A bundles the dataset, design matrix and linear model into one definition of the regression model with Sigma covariance and noise epsilon. Paper B splits the same setup across three definitions: dataset D, design/target matrices (X, Y), and linear model f(x)=x.beta. The substantive content (covariate-target pairs, linear predictor on R^D) is identical.

Both define the empirical second-moment / kernel matrices. Paper A uses hat-Sigma = (1/n) X^T X (empirical covariance) and X X^T (kernel matrix); Paper B uses X^T X (second-moment matrix) and X X^T (Gram matrix). Same two matrices, same role in the regression solutions, with only an n-normalisation convention difference and a remark in B (RP459.3) that 'second-moment' is a more accurate name without centering.

Paper A's DP458.7 defines the ridge estimator hat-theta = (X^T X + n lambda I)^{-1} X^T y and ProbP458.1 states the corresponding ridge optimization. Paper B's TP459.1 gives the underparameterized OLS closed-form (X^T X)^{-1} X^T Y with ProbP459.1 the matching least-squares optimization. These coincide at lambda=0 in Bach's notation; the OLS estimator is the lambda-->0 limit of Bach's ridge estimator, so this is the same object up to ridge regularisation. The small difference (B does not include the ridge term) prevents 'analogous' downgrade because the formulas are literally specialisations of one another.

Paper A defines the minimum-norm interpolant of y under the random-projection model XS eta (DP458.8 / ProbP458.2). Paper B defines the standard minimum-norm interpolant of y under X beta (ProbP459.2) with closed form X^T (X X^T)^{-1} Y (TP459.2). Both pick the smallest-norm interpolant of the training data; they play the same role in the over-parameterised regime. They are analogous (not exact) because Paper A multiplies on the right by a random Gaussian sketch S in R^{d x m}, while Paper B works with the unprojected design directly.

Paper A's DP458.2 sets up the bias-variance decomposition of the excess risk R(hat-theta) = (hat-theta - theta_*)^T Sigma (hat-theta - theta_*). Paper B's TP459.3 / TP459.4 give the corresponding finite-sample decomposition of the prediction error y_hat_test - y_test^* into a bias term and a singular-mode variance term sum 1/sigma_r (x_test.v_r)(u_r.E). Both are bias/variance decompositions of generalisation error; they differ in how they realise the variance term (asymptotic equivalent vs. SVD per-mode sum).

df_1(kappa) = tr[Sigma(Sigma+kappa I)^{-1}] and df_2(kappa) = tr[Sigma^2(Sigma+kappa I)^{-2}] are central to Paper A's analysis (effective dimensionalities driving the asymptotic equivalents). Paper B never introduces effective dimensionalities of this kind; its closest tool is the singular-value spectrum of X handled mode-by-mode.

The Stieltjes transform hat-phi(z) of the empirical kernel matrix is a paper-A-specific object (the random-matrix-theory engine of Bach's analysis). Paper B works directly with the SVD X = U Sigma V^T and never invokes Stieltjes transforms or resolvents.

Self-induced regularization kappa(lambda) = 1/phi(-lambda) is unique to Paper A. It plays the role of an implicit ridge penalty produced by the random design itself. Paper B has no analogue: it works in finite samples via SVD truncation rather than via an implicit regulariser.
Asymptotic equivalent tr[hat-Sigma(hat-Sigma+lambda I)^{-1}] ~ tr[Sigma(Sigma+kappa(lambda) I)^{-1}] is a classical RMT identity used by Paper A; Paper B does no asymptotic random matrix theory.
The self-consistent Stieltjes equation 1/phi(z) + z = gamma * integral sigma dmu / (1 + sigma phi(z)) is a paper-A-specific tool. Paper B has no Stieltjes machinery.

Closed-form kappa(lambda) for isotropic Sigma is paper-A-specific. Paper B alludes to Marchenko-Pastur in ClP459.2 to argue that the smallest non-zero singular value bottoms out at N=P=D, but it does not derive a closed-form analogue of kappa(lambda).
Paper A's main spectral-equivalent proposition (linear and quadratic trace equivalents for hat-Sigma) is a core RMT contribution with no counterpart in Paper B's SVD-based analysis.
Kernel-form spectral equivalents are paper-A-specific, used internally to handle the right-multiplication by S in the random-projection setting.

Both compute bias and variance for an over-parameterised linear regression. Paper A gives the asymptotic ridge bias and variance in terms of df_2(kappa(lambda)) and 1/(1 - df_2/n); Paper B gives a finite-sample SVD expression sum 1/sigma_r (x_test.v_r)(u_r.E) for the variance and a (X^T(XX^T)^{-1}X - I)beta_* term for the bias. The conceptual content matches (variance dominated by small singular values / inverse degrees of freedom; bias related to the projection deficit), but the formulas and proof techniques differ markedly, so 'analogous' is the right granularity.

Paper A's PrP458.4 is the formal random-projection double-descent theorem: under-parameterised variance ~ sigma^2 m/(n-m), over-parameterised variance contains the divergent sigma^2 n/(m-n) term that produces the spike at m=n. Paper B's TP459.4 + ClP459.1 + ClP459.2 articulate the same spike informally via three factors: small sigma_r at the interpolation threshold (where 1/sigma_r blows up just as 1/(n-m) does in Paper A), residual projection, and test-feature projection. Both identify the same divergence mechanism; Paper A quantifies it asymptotically, Paper B explains it geometrically.

Both papers invoke the Marchenko-Pastur distribution. Paper A cites MP as the limiting spectral distribution recovered when Sigma = sigma I (TP458.1). Paper B cites MP in ClP459.2 to argue that the smallest non-zero singular value is driven to its lowest value at N=P=D. Same external result; in Paper A it is an explicitly external citation, in Paper B it is invoked informally inside a paper-original claim. Match recorded because the underlying cited result is the same.
Hanson-Wright is a key concentration tool in Paper A (used in PP458.3 to control the Delta term). Paper B does not invoke any concentration inequality.
Paper A's proof of the random-design ridge bias-variance via trace equivalents has no counterpart in Paper B.

Paper A's proof of the random-projection double-descent proposition (separate under- and over-parameterised arguments, expand w.r.t. X then S, etc.) is paper-A-specific; Paper B never proves the corresponding asymptotic theorem.
Proof of the self-consistent Stieltjes equation following Silverstein has no counterpart in Paper B.
Proof of Propositions 1 and 2 (linear and quadratic spectral equivalents) is paper-A-specific.
Paper A's isotropic-covariance Marchenko-Pastur worked example is auxiliary; the closest object on the B side is ClP459.2's informal MP-based argument, but that is more an assertion than an example.

Paper A's Example 4 (1/k eigenvalues, d=400, n=200) is its primary numerical illustration of double descent on a non-isotropic spectrum. Paper B's ExP459.1-4 are its empirical illustrations of double descent (a polynomial-regression toy and three real tabular datasets). Same goal (visualise the test-error spike at the interpolation threshold), different setups: Paper A's is a synthetic non-isotropic spectrum carefully aligned with its theory; Paper B's are real datasets (WHO, California Housing, Diabetes) plus a 1-D polynomial toy. Coupling them as a many-to-many illustrative cluster.

Both state the underparameterised least-squares (or ridge) optimisation problem. Paper A includes the lambda||theta||^2 penalty term; Paper B states the unpenalised version. Identical objects up to the explicit ridge term. (This match overlaps with the DP458.7 <-> TP459.1 entry above; we keep both because the proposition / optimisation framings are listed as separate node types in the inputs.)

Both are minimum-norm least-squares problems. Paper A's variant is over the projected design XS (interpolation when m>n); Paper B's variant is over X directly (interpolation when D>N). Same conceptual problem; different parameterisation due to the random-projection layer S in Paper A.

Paper A's six high-dimensional asymptotic assumptions (sub-Gaussian design, d/n -> gamma, spectral measure convergence, signal spectral measure, sub-Gaussian projection, m/n -> delta) have no counterpart in Paper B, which works in finite-samples without an asymptotic limit and makes essentially no distributional assumptions on X beyond random features with finite second moments.

Paper B explicitly defines the over/underparameterised regimes and the interpolation threshold N=P. Paper A uses these regimes (e.g. m<n vs m>n in PrP458.4) but never names them as a separate definition; the concept is implicit in its case-split.

Paper B's polynomial feature map (Legendre polynomials) is specific to its tutorial polynomial-regression example. Paper A has no analogue; its features are the raw covariates x_i in R^d optionally multiplied by a random Gaussian S.

Paper B's notation Y = X beta_* + E with residuals E (which can be noise OR model-class misspecification) is a finite-sample formulation. Paper A's noise epsilon in DP458.1 is purely additive noise; it does not bundle in a 'model-class residual' interpretation. Adjacent but not the same conceptual object.
Paper B's Lagrangian derivation of the min-norm interpolant is a textbook derivation of TP459.2. Paper A simply states the closed form without a Lagrangian proof.

Paper B's SVD-substitution proof of the prediction-error decomposition is paper-B-specific; it is the engine of Paper B's three-factor analysis. Paper A's proofs proceed through Stieltjes transforms instead.
Paper B's prediction equations y_hat_test = x_test . hat-beta for both regimes are auxiliary algebraic statements that Paper A does not explicitly write in this form.

Paper B's ClP459.3 lists necessary conditions (small sigma_r present, test point not in leading subspace, residuals nonzero) under which double descent fails. Paper A's PrP458.4 asymptotic formulas implicitly recover the same intuition: the divergence at m=n disappears under ridge regularization (kappa(lambda)>0 keeps things bounded), which is one of B's conditions. The mapping is intuitive but not a direct theorem-to-theorem correspondence.

Paper B's polynomial regression sweep (Legendre features, sweep P from 1 to 200, target y(x) = 2x + cos(25x)) is a tutorial visualisation algorithm. Paper A does not include any such procedural sweep; its illustrations are direct numerical evaluations of the asymptotic equivalents.
Paper B's OLS sweep over N on real tabular datasets is specific to its empirical methodology. Paper A has no real-data experiments.

Paper B's three-factor ablation procedure (cut small singular values, project test features, linearise targets) is its principal experimental contribution. Paper A has no analogous ablation, since its theoretical framework does not isolate three independent causal factors of the spike.
